utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Good morning, ladies and gentlemen. Is this a new pattern now, you already kept the blinds closed? Is that what you do now? (Pause.) Now, we have before us listed three motions, which we have scheduled for this morning. We will start with the first one: this is a request for a formal finding of the Trial Chamber that the accused Landzo is fit to stand trial; the second, the motion for extension of time in which to file motions pursuant to Rule 73A(3) and relief from waiver; the third, motion for leave to file motion to exclude evidence in connection with Delic; the fourth, the motion to exclude evidence that is filed by counsel for Mucic. Now, we will start with the first one before the Trial Chamber: the question for our finding about the fitness to stand trial. That is a little bit of an enigma to me, why the prosecution is asking for that, but I suppose ...

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Mrs McHenry will speak to that, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honours. We did not -- we do not suggest that this is, as far as we know, even a contested issue, but just so that the record was very clear, so that if there is subsequently appeal, there is no question about it, the prosecution believe that it would be appropriate for the record to formally have a finding that the accused is fit to stand trial. Previously this issue had been raised. The accused was examined. Two doctors found he was fit to stand trial and one doctor found he was not, in his opinion. We believe that the more well reasoned and the more convincing of the findings of the two doctors are the doctors that found that the accused was fit to stand trial. We believe that the accused's conduct, which even the Trial Chamber can observe during court -- conferring with his counsel, behaving appropriately -- such things indicate that he is fit to stand trial, and we assume by the fact that the proceedings have been on-going that there is an implicit finding by both this Chamber and an agreement by the defence that he is fit to stand trial, but without making it a significant deal, we just thought it would be best if there was a formal finding, even if it is an oral, one sentence finding, that the accused is fit to stand trial. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honours. Just very briefly, I am puzzled, like Judge Karibi Whyte is puzzled, by this motion, since we have filed no motion contending that Mr. Landzo is not competent to stand trial. It is quite unusual for the Prosecutor to ask for such a finding when it has not been asserted by the defence in the first place. Beyond that we have nothing further to say with regard to it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I think this is the end of the matter. We will give a Ruling later. There is nothing to pursue in this matter. The next motion is that filed by counsel for Landzo pursuant to Rule 73A and relief from waiver. I think counsel for Landzo can speak to that motion.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honours. The basic heart of the motion that was filed is based upon the proposition that even though the record of the Landzo interview shows that he had counsel present at the time of the interview, and even though Mr. Landzo was advised at least to some extent by those conducting the interview of what his rights were, the contention that I wish to make, if I am permitted to file a motion to suppress, is that neither of those were sufficient to protect his rights. It is based upon the following proposition. In most countries one could not represent an individual charged with a serious crime without first passing a Bar examination regarding all the law and the rules and procedures covering those kinds of proceedings that they would be appearing in. Once that attorney has passed such a Bar examination and been admitted to the Bar, only then is he or she permitted to appear on behalf of an accused and advise an accused as to what he or she should do. The situation that existed at the time the statement was taken from Mr. Landzo was a situation in which he was represented by a very capable and honourable attorney by the name of Mustafa Brackovic. Mustafa Brackovic's training was in law and procedure in the former Yugoslavia. Any examination that he took to become a lawyer in the former Yugoslavia would have been based on Yugoslavian law and procedure. My understanding, and I would be prepared to prove, if I am permitted to file the motion, is that under Yugoslavian law a defendant is expected to make a statement -- an accused is expected to make a statement -- and that that statement can never be used against that accused without the accused's permission. Under many of the civil law continental systems it is, in fact, a detriment to the accused if he fails to make such a statement. The making of a statement by an accused, if he is convicted of the offence for which he is charged, goes a long way towards mitigating punishment because he made such a statement. It may cut punishment in half because he made such a statement. That is an entirely different procedure, dramatically different procedure, from what obtains under the common law and in the United States and the United Kingdom and other places where the common law is applied. I think the matter is especially a problem because of the presence at the interview of Mr. Landzo of Ms. Teresa McHenry. Ms. Teresa McHenry is a Prosecutor in this case and comes to this court from the United States Department of Justice. I am convinced, and will be prepared to prove, if I am allowed to, that she was fully aware at the time this interview was taken of the difference that I have described between the training of the honourable Mustafa Brackovic and the kind of training and experience that she received in her law school education and her Bar examination and in her experience with the Department of Justice: it is the almost inevitable case under US law that the only way that a statement is taken from an accused is either it is done before the accused has counsel, or if done after the accused has counsel, pursuant to a plea agreement that has been entered into with the prosecution, where that accused may become a prosecution witness and testify against other defendants similarly charged. It is my contention that, having this knowledge and having this experience, it was at the very least the duty of Ms. McHenry to tell Mr. Brackovic, knowing his background, that before advising his client about whether or not to make a statement that he should at least consult with a lawyer from a common law jurisdiction as to the ordinary procedure in those jurisdictions when accuseds are called upon by the prosecution to make a statement. She failed to do so. The situation that Mr. Landzo found himself in the day that the prosecutors came to take his statement was a situation that no defendant could ever find himself in in the United Kingdom or in the United States. It could not happen in either of those two jurisdictions, because it could not happen without counsel agreeing, and that counsel would have to be counsel that was admitted to the Bar of those jurisdictions. To turn it the other way around, if I were to appear in the former Yugoslavia by myself to represent someone accused of an offence in the former Yugoslavia, my initial reaction, when called upon to decide whether my accused should make a statement to the prosecution or not, would be absolutely not. Under no circumstances do you give a statement to the Prosecution. If I took that position without consulting with Yugoslavian lawyers, I would be taking the wrong position, and I would not be serving my client well, but I would not know that I would not be serving my client well. I would believe that I was doing the right thing. Mr. Mustafa Brackovic, when he advised Esad Landzo, believed that he was doing the right thing. It turns out that that is not the case. It turns out that the statement can, in fact, be used against Mr. Landzo, all other things being equal. Mr. Landzo, of course, at the time was 20 or 21 years old, with absolutely no experience of any kind with the law, and was absolutely dependent upon his attorney, Mr. Mustafa Brackovic, to advise him properly. Please understand -- I need the Tribunal to understand very clearly that I am not in any manner attacking the competence of the honourable Mustafa Brackovic. He is an extremely competent lawyer and any accused in the former Yugoslavia that would have him as an attorney would be well served, absolutely. It is only in the situation that he found himself here that he was unable to give the kind of advice that any common law lawyer would automatically have given to Esad Landzo with regard to giving the statement. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Just a minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Was your client advised that he had a right to remain silent and that if he made a statement, it would be used in evidence against him?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. He was absolutely advised of both of those things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Would that not put his counsel on guard?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Maybe; maybe not. My client had come from a situation in Yugoslavia where, if he did not give a statement, he would likely be beaten. He had been here a very, very short period of time. He was in a new surrounding, in a new prison. He had no idea what the situation would be here. So to the extent that he made any kind of a decision himself about whether or not to give a statement, I submit to your Honours that that was not an informed decision, that it was based on a lot of factors that turned out to be not true: a fear factor, advice from his lawyer, all the things that were not true, and when you waive rights, when you waive rights like the prosecution is suggesting that my client waived here, it is not just the fact of a waiver that counts; it is whether or not it is an intelligent and knowing waiver of those rights. I submit to your Honours that there was not an intelligent and knowing waiver of those rights in this matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Actually it appears you are basing your argument mainly on the protection given to your client by his counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Absolutely. It is being based on that, but let me say once again that it is not an attack on his counsel. His counsel was doing exactly what he was trained to do and what he knew to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: I agree. I consider that. Are you saying only those trained in the common law are qualified to act as counsel to accused persons in these circumstances?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Absolutely not, your Honour. I could not say that with a straight face sitting next to Mme Residovic, because I have watched her performance and it has been exemplary. What I am saying is when the prosecution seeks to take a statement from the accused, if that accused is represented by an attorney who is unfamiliar with common law procedure, the prosecution has an additional duty to advise the defendant, the accused and the accused's attorney. It is like if Mr. Brackovic were to go to the United States to represent a defendant in the United States. The courts of the United States would not even permit him to appear on behalf of a defendant unless he had obtained local counsel familiar with the local procedure and rules. He could not appear alone to do that. This court should adopt some kind of a procedure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Have you looked at Rule 44 on the appointment of qualified counsel?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, I have and I am very familiar with the Rule, and I am totally in agreement that Mr. Brackovic was appointed in accordance with that Rule and absolutely properly appointed in accordance with that Rule.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: What then makes any lawyer so appointed incompetent to discharge his duties to his client?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I really need to say to your Honour that I am not suggesting that Mr. Brackovic was incompetent to discharge his duties. I am only suggesting to your Honours that there were matters that he did not know, that he would have known had he gotten even five minutes of advice from Ms. McHenry to talk to a common law lawyer before he advised his client to give a statement. I think Ms. McHenry took unfair advantage of Mr. Brackovic by not giving him that kind of advice. She knew the background he came from. She knew he did not have the grounding in common law procedure that lawyers from common law jurisdictions would have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Actually this is the basis of your argument.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It is the basis of my argument, and please keep in mind, your Honour, all I am asking to do at this point is to file a motion to suppress. I am not arguing whether or not there should be a suppression.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Your argument should be weighty enough in terms of the first application.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I hope it is weighty enough for this court to permit me to file a motion to suppress, which we can then hear at a later time. I would propose to put on some evidence to support it regarding statements I have made out of my own mouth here today that I think I would need to prove to the Tribunal to consider that motion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: You are quite right to say before a waiver can be made the person making the waiver must be fully aware of what his rights are. That is quite right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Can we hear the prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Thank you. I will let Ms. McHenry answer the severe allegations put forward against her, but before I do that, I would put one question to Mr. Ackerman. What, Mr. Ackerman, would you have founded your motion on if I had been present instead of Ms. McHenry? I am from the civil law system and I am before a international court and not before a US court and I am living by the standard of this Statute and these Rules. What could you have put forward as argument if I had, instead of Ms. Teresa McHenry, been sitting there with Mr. Brackovic that day when the statement was taken from Mr. Landzo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: But you come from a civil law system where no beating takes place.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: I beg your pardon?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: You come from a civil law system where the accused is not beaten for not making a statement. That is what he is suggesting.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: This suggestion is unfounded. How could it be put forward before this Tribunal that a thing like that could be imagined before this Tribunal? . I am waiting for your answer, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Strictly speaking I do not know. It depends on -- questions are not put to counsel directly. If you are doing so through the court --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: I do so through the court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Or in making your submissions, you can do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: I make the submission --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: It can be part of your submissions and he will answer this.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: I ask you, your Honour, to put forward my question to Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: No, I do not think so. After your submissions there will be answers to those submissions.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, just briefly, and other than to say that the allegations against me and, in fact, I think, against all civil law attorneys are in their own turn unfair. I will not specifically respond to the specific attacks made on me and my integrity and conduct in this case. With respect to the merits of this situation, I will point out that what the accused is, as your Honours have pointed out, suggesting is that all civil law attorneys are in effect incompetent to give advice to their clients in this Tribunal because this is a common law Tribunal. I would take issue with both those allegations. This is not a common law Tribunal. It is a mixture of both civil and common law. For instance, we do not have a jury. That is one of the most obvious things. It is not the prosecution's duty and, in fact, it is really not the prosecution's business to interfere. In the same way that I would not suggest to a civil law attorney how to conduct their defence, or to an accused, I would not suggest to an accused that it is somehow improper to have two common law attorneys instead of a civil law attorney. It is absolutely not the prosecution's business to give unsolicited advice. The Rules were set up by these judges of this Tribunal, and, in fact, even by the UN with the Statute, in which certain rules were clearly laid out, and it is, of course, understood that there is no lawyer who comes from this particular system, unless at this point we get some of the Tadic lawyers, because it is a new system. That is why the Rules are set out, and with respect to certain things, including the accused's rights with respect to interviews, the Rules are so very clear. The Rules were made such that anyone, no matter what their system and what their background, can understand what is being said. In this case the Rules were followed in every respect. I will also point out that Mr. Landzo had been in The Hague for over a month, approximately a month, I believe a month and two days, prior to his giving the statement. I do not believe that there can be any allegation that he thought he would be beaten if he did not give one. I also believe that it is clear that defence counsel consulted with Mr. Landzo before there was a decision made to do this. I also point out as a matter of fact, although we emphasise that the law in any country is not controlling, that it is not correct that in Yugoslavia, at least as experts in Yugoslavian law have told us -- it is not correct that people are required to give statements, nor is it correct that if an accused gives a statement to, for instance, the investigating magistrate, that he can later decide whether or not to use that statement. My fellow colleagues also tell me that it is the same thing with respect in other civil law systems. It is not correct that an accused can always choose that. I will also just point out that even before Mr. Landzo decided to provide a statement, he had learned -- well, the defence counsel of Delalic had filed a motion seeking to exclude the first statement made by Mr. Delalic, in which it is abundantly clear that there is a difference between Yugoslavian -- there may be -- there are allegations -- between Yugoslavian law and Tribunal law, and that was also known, and what the accused -- what the defence is doing is suggesting that what happens in the US, in which it may have been -- it may be that an accused would choose not to do so, must apply. I would point out that in this case this is not the US and, in fact, it may not even have been a decision -- I mean, a bad decision, but in any event it was an informed, knowing and voluntary decision, and just because new counsel comes in and has a different opinion, maybe based correctly or incorrectly on his own system, means that the initial waiver was somehow improper, involuntary or unknowing. To the contrary, the record is very clear, and it is conceded that the Rules and the warnings, which are obvious on their face, were given and understood by all counsel. I will also just specifically with respect to the good cause motion point out that there has been a significant length of time in which common law attorneys have been part of this case, and though we reject entirely the notion that civil law attorneys cannot understand, or an accused himself cannot understand, the clear meaning of these rules, it has been the matter for several months that a common law attorney has been associated with this case, and to allow two months or more into trial allegations such as these, which we think are clearly lacking in merit on their face, to constitute good cause would really be a miscarriage of justice. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have just two very brief matters to give you in response. The first is that it is now clear from what Ms. McHenry has told you that there is a factual dispute about what the law was in the former Yugoslavia, and that can only be resolved by documents or witnesses, if I am permitted to file the motion to suppress, and I would propose to do that, if the motion is permitted. Ms. McMurrey (sic) also told you that it is not the job of the prosecution to give the defendant, the accused, unsolicited advice, but if you read the very beginning of Mr. Landzo's statement, that is exactly what happened. Mr. Landzo did not solicit any advice from the prosecution at all, but the prosecution did give advice. That advice was, and it is not as clear, I do not think, as it should be -- that advice was: "You are not obliged to say anything unless you wish to do so, but whatever you say will be recorded and may be given in evidence."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: There is a duty --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I am sorry, your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: There is a duty for anybody interviewing a suspect or an accused person to tell him those things. It is not necessarily advice.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It is unsolicited advice. There is a Rule saying it must be given and must be given in a way the defendant understands it. There is also a Rule saying they must advise he will be assisted by counsel and counsel will be appointed for him if he cannot afford counsel. All I am suggesting to this court is, in the process of giving that unsolicited advice, I think there should have been some additional unsolicited advice that I have already suggested to the court. Now I understand that my colleague, Mr. Greaves, would like to address the court regarding a perspective that may be different from mine in this regard. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: In respect of this motion?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I really want to wear my amicus hat this morning and assist the court with what I hope are helpful observations. I am not taking part in the substance of the argument. If the court would welcome such assistance, I would like to give it, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: You can do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Your Honours, it is entirely right what the prosecution says about the Rules of Procedure and Evidence in this court, that they are drawn from two of the great traditions of law, the common law and the civil law. Anybody who, as I have, over the last eight weeks, learned a considerable amount about the civil law -- any common lawyer in those circumstances will understand that both the common law and the civil law have considerable advantages and considerable disadvantages, and my respect for civil lawyers and civil law grows by the day. There are some aspects of it that I do not care for as a common lawyer, but that is another matter altogether. The fact is our Rules of Evidence and Procedure are drawn from both systems, although it might be said that the common law has had a greater input into the Rules than perhaps the civil law has. That is perhaps an argument for academics in due course. However, the Rules that have been drawn up for the protection of suspects in connection with their rights to counsel and what should happen during the course of interviews and so on and so forth are, in my submission, drawn almost exclusively from the common law tradition and any common lawyer picking up the Rules of Evidence and Procedure in this Tribunal would instantly be familiar with those particular aspects of the Rules. In my submission it is very likely, therefore, that this Tribunal would want to look at the way in which common law jurisdictions -- for assistance common law jurisdictions interpret and apply such laws in order to come to their own determination as to what the Rules mean and how it should be applied by this Tribunal applying its own Rules. I go on to say this: The consequences of the warnings that are given typically in common law jurisdictions are both very important and are not straightforward, and indeed in most jurisdictions there is quite a degree of subtlety to them. It comes to this: where you have someone from a civil law jurisdiction, those subtleties and the degree of importance and the consequences and effects of the warnings and the failures to give them, if those take place, are matters which a common lawyer is, I have to say, very much better placed than his civil law colleague in giving advice to the defendant when he is being interviewed, and what he should say, whether he should say anything at all. So plainly the proposition that is being put is a civil lawyer is just as competent to advise them as a common lawyer. It may not be seen to be entirely right, and I hope that the court will bear that in mind when coming to its determination on this issue. Can I add this: there has been some exchange of views about the duties of various members of the prosecution team, the defence team and so forth. I do not enter into those. Can I just give your Honours my experience as a practitioner in the courts of England and Wales? If I was to come across a young member of the Bar who was plainly inexperienced and plainly about to do something to the detriment of his client, I would not take advantage of that. Instead, I would take him or her into one corner and give him some sound advice, as the Prosecutor -- sorry, not as the Prosecutor but as an officer of the court and a member of my profession, and say to that person: "Look, you are about to make a serious mistake which is going to harm your client. My advice to you is either to seek advice from another member of the Bar or to do this." I would regard that as my duty, because my duty as a prosecutor is not to ensure a conviction at all costs, but to ensure that right and justice is done. I hope that does not sound pompous, but it was something that was drilled into me from the very first day I joined this profession over 20 years ago. It might be suggested if that is accepted as a proposition, then my learned friend for the prosecution, Ms. McHenry, might be thought to have a duty over and above that of being a Prosecutor. If there is anything I can assist you with any further, I will, of course, do so, but that is all I have to say. MS. RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): Your Honours, may I join in the discussion of this issue, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, you can. MS. RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): Like my honourable colleagues, I also believe that we should ensure that this trial is fair and just in regard to all the defendants. For this reason the defence of Mr. Delalic attempted on several occasions to indicate to this Trial Chamber certain lacks and deficiencies in the rules like Rule 89B. As we all understand, this Tribunal is not bound by the international law, and we all have to respect the fact and appreciate that we are all coming from a certain legal tradition, and if this Trial Chamber wants this trial to be fair and just, it should bear this in mind, so that the trial should proceed in such a manner. I did not understand the submission of my colleague, Mr. Ackerman, as a critique or a comment on incompetence of all the lawyers who are coming from a different legal system. I think that he was just trying to point to this Trial Chamber some things that ourselves and our clients have done; it is not ignoratia legis nocet. In other words, we did these things because we did not know certain things and this could be detrimental to our clients. We may have done certain things precisely because we may know certain things quite well, because they are part of our tradition, our legal systems in the countries that we are coming from. Besides the motion that we filed to exclude the first statement given by Mr. Delalic in Vienna, we were expecting to be given an opportunity to discuss these arguments in terms of voir dire, where we would call an expert in the criminal law from the territory of the former Yugoslavia, not from Bosnia and Herzegovina or even Croatia and Serbia, who may have been parties to the conflict, which this case is covering, but rather from Slovenia. So I think it would be extremely important that our colleagues would be given an opportunity to produce such experts, persons who would explain what the legal practice and legal experience means as rights to the lawyer and a warning of the lawyer to his client as to what he should or should not do. Now I would like to respond to the comments made by my colleagues from the prosecution. I myself spent part of my career as a Prosecutor, and I am able to submit to you, and we can produce experts to confirm this, that any statement given to the police or the investigating magistrate is immediately sealed and can never be used either to the advantage or -- either in the interest or against the accused unless the accused explicitly asks for that. When we first started working on this case, we did not know every detail about the procedures. So I would like to request of the Trial Chamber and in order to respect the Article 21 to allow this argument to be presented so that in the future we would have a different way of presenting our case. Then, bearing in mind all this, the defence of Mr. Delalic submitted a motion on 28th December asking for amendment of certain Rules to amend the procedure, because a number of issues, when I present them, you may not understand them, and when my colleagues from the common law systems present them, I may not understand them. In a hearing at which you presided, when I asked about the active role of my client, which I understood to mean that he could actively become involved in the case in confronting witnesses, asking questions of the co-defendants, the ultimate Ruling was that he could not do it unless he does it through my mouth as his defence representative. Again I would like to point out our colleagues from the common law systems, I do not think they have critiqued us. I just think they are pointing to the differences within the legal systems and this all points to the issue of the fair and just trial. Thank you, your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Ms. Residovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, since I have almost an identical motion coming up next, if I can talk that now, and we could possibly save the Tribunal a little time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: You mean whether you are contributing to this motion or you are moving your own motion?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, it is essentially the same thing. I think we can probably save a little time if we did them together, or at least let me state my position, help on this motion and at the same time save a bunch of time on the next motion, rather than having to repeat it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: You can combine them since they still come to the same thing, although they might differ in certain respects.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, first I would adopt what Judge Ackerman had to say with a couple of additions and deletions. The first thing is: Rule 73 provides that these motions need to be filed within 60 days after the initial appearance. One of the statements they want to introduce was taken more than 60 days after the initial appearance. Under that strict application of the Rule you could never try to exclude it. So the Rule has to have some flexibility there. Secondly, we have talked about our Rules here coming from different sources and they have, but they did not just spring full blown. For instance, Rule 73 is very, very familiar to me as an American practitioner, because it reads almost identical to Federal Rule of Criminal Procedure 12, I believe. They are almost copied from each other. The same thing with Rule 42. The warnings in Rule 42 read a whole lot like our warnings in the case of Miranda versus Arizona from the United States Supreme Court. In fact, I am told, although I have not read it, in response to a motion from Mr. Delalic last year the prosecution cited Miranda a lot of times and relied on Miranda. Now, with that said, I will be real frank with the court as an officer of the court. When I got here and found that Mr. Delic had given a couple of statements, the first thing I did was uttered an obscenity and just set it aside until I started thinking -- talking to Judge Ackerman after he arrived here a few weeks ago. What we have is a situation where for one reason or another apparently the former Yugoslavia adopted a procedure where a statement made to the police -- by the way, I think we need to draw a distinction between the police and the investigating magistrate, who are two different parties -- as I understand the law in the Yugoslavia it has to do with a statement to the police and not the investigating magistrate, which is a court proceeding. I don't know why the former Yugoslavia adopted that rule. It probably has to do to some great extent with the history of that country and the history of that part of the world and possibly abuses of human rights that occurred at some time in the history of Yugoslavia and other Eastern European countries, but suffice to say that that was the rule. Sitting next to me is my good friend, my lead counsel. He is a fine lawyer and I would not want anybody to think that he was not a fine lawyer or that I thought that he was not a fine lawyer, but the fact is he was thrown into a situation involving a legal system with entirely different procedures and, especially as it applies to statements to investigators, something that is entirely different from what he was used to. Without violating the attorney-client privilege, there is a statement by Mr. Delic attached to our motion that, after consulting with counsel, he believed that the situation was similar to that in the former Yugoslavia. Now we attempted to get that sworn to, but apparently the Registrar did not feel they could swear him to that. He is willing to file that as an affidavit. With that said, I think we need to take a look at the voluntariness of any kind of waiver of his rights under Rule 42, and what is it, 66, the Rule having to do with questioning of accused. Rule 63. Again I have to dance around this a little bit because of the attorney-client privilege and I do not want to violate that. I think that Mr. Delic, if called upon for the limited purpose of testifying as to this, would testify consistent with his written statement. Finally, without trying to even come close to making a personal attack on my good friend Ms. McHenry, as I understand it, each one of us here, as lawyers, are bound by our ethical proceedings by our country, as our licensing authority. So I am, for instance, bound by what the Texas Supreme Court says is my ethical obligations and Mr. Greaves would be bound by what the ethical considerations would be in the United Kingdom, etc. Well, our American Bar Association has model rules and those model rules have been adopted by just about every state in the country. One of the things they talk about is the duty of a Prosecutor. What they say is that the duty of a Prosecutor is not to gain convictions but to see that justice is done. Again I am not trying to make an attack on anyone's ethics, but at some point, when someone is obviously unfamiliar with what is going on, either we have an obligation to say "Time out", or what occurs on the other side of it is we may have to take a look at the advice that was given and to see whether that advice by an attorney is the proper advice. If it is not, then we have to see what the ramifications of that are. If the ramifications were that a waiver is not a knowing, intelligent waiver, then we have to deal with that. With that, your Honour, unless the court has some questions, I think I will just sit down and try to save the court -- like I say, I am just trying to save the court a little bit of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: If you have other things to say, let us hear it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am done.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, again first let me state that the prosecution, myself included, but lead counsel and everyone else certainly agrees that the prosecution has a duty to truth and justice and not to gain a conviction at any cost, but we do not believe that there is anything here that suggests in any way, shape or form that there has been any straying from that fundamental principle, which is that the prosecution, both as officers of the court, as officers of their own system, and even as members of the Tribunal, have an obligation to ensure that justice is done. That is certainly our aim, and we have demonstrated in many ways and there is nothing in this case which should cast doubt on that, because in effect what the defence is saying is that civil law attorneys, or at least attorneys from the former Yugoslavia, are not competent to give proper advice in this case, that they are not competent and really that accused are not competent to waive their own rights. We think that is entirely incorrect. Had the judges wanted to state in the Rules: "No accused can ever give a statement because it is unfair", or: "No accused can ever give a statement unless they first talk with a US lawyer", or something like that -- they did not. The Rules state very clearly that an accused must be informed of his rights, and that the accused must knowingly and voluntarily waive those rights. We believe that the record will show that was done in this case. The fact that attorneys may have come and have different strategy decisions which may or may not be right even is not a reason to do it. I will also point out, although certainly as Yugoslavia law, whatever it is, is not controlling at this court, and there had been some discussion whether or not this Tribunal should adopt the Rules and Procedure of Yugoslavia and this Tribunal has said: "No. We are going to adopt fundamental rights which can be understood by anyone, no matter what their system", and the Tribunal has done this. Those rights were followed in all respects in this case. We do not -- I would also point out that the rights, specifically with respect to the rights of the accused, do not come from common law countries, although they may be familiar to people from common law countries, because we have similar things; they come from the European Convention of Human Rights. So they may also come from the US, but it is not as from the US or England and even other common law countries. They are unique. The fundamental rights come from the European Convention of Human Rights, which apply in European and most other countries. Specifically with respect to Mr. Delic, let me respond to that for one minute. I assume your Honours have received our responses both to Mr. Landzo's and Mr. Delic's, which were filed yesterday. If not, I can go into our response in more detail, but in general we do not want to just repeat everything we said in our motion. With respect to Mr. Delic, as with respect to Mr. Landzo, the issue is what constitutes good cause, and certainly the prosecution would agree if a statement is made 60 days after the initial appearance that could constitute good cause, for instance within reason some period of time close to when the statement was made. The second statement of Mr. Delic, which was made at his request, was made in January, in the beginning of January. In fact, counsel, as he himself has conceded, came soon thereafter in January, and had they wanted to raise it then they could have. What has happened is a new strategy decision has been made again without saying what in the end would turn out to be best for the accused -- I do not think anyone can know that now -- and so they have decided to try to argue good cause. The asserted reason given in Mr. Delic's motion was a ruling by this Trial Chamber that involuntary statements are admissible. Without repeating everything, we do not believe that this was a new finding by the Trial Chamber. We believe that it is a fundamental principle of law, and had Mr. Delic or any of the accused wished to make a claim based on this statement, they could have, and no one would have argued that the law was anything other than that. So we do not believe that anything they recently have constitute good cause. We again, with respect to Mr. Delic, so the record is clear -- both interviews of Mr. Delic were done in full accordance with the Tribunal Rules of Procedure. The accused and counsel were informed of all their rights. This is all on the record. They were specifically told this statement could be used in evidence. If there were any questions, misunderstandings, confusion, they could have been asked, they could have been followed up, but they were not, because the accused and his counsel voluntarily chose to waive them. We point out some specific facts in our motion such as even by the time of the second interview the prosecution had already told the accused that they would use his statement in evidence against him. That had already been done, and we believe that there cannot be any credible showing that Mr. Delic's statement was anything other than voluntary, knowing and intelligent. Excuse me, your Honours. My civil law colleagues also just state that it is not incorrect in most civil law systems that the accused is expected to talk and it is not true that the accused can decide whether his statement will be used or not, and that the statements also made to the Prosecution here should not be compared with statements given to the police in civil law countries. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, a couple of quick things in response. First, I think that the court will, if it -- will hear some evidence from Mr. Mucic that he was given some warnings by a Magistrate in Vienna that essentially said: "If you don't make a statement to the police, things are going to go hard on you." Austria is a common law country -- excuse me -- civil law country. Secondly, it has been my experience, and I have a case involving my law firm that was just delivered to me Monday which supports this, that when there is a mistake by a lawyer and that mistake affects the trial, the courts tend to try and go and fix it. The case I am thinking of is a case on May 1st of this year where a Federal Judge in my jurisdiction vacated a death sentence on one of our clients because the trial lawyer did not understand the application of the law in his trial in 1982 -- I believe it was 1982. I am willing to provide a copy of the Decision to the court. It is in my hotel room. I can go over at lunch and get it copied. What we are asking for is a chance to show if there was a misunderstanding of the law on the part of counsel and whether that misunderstanding of the law led my client to waive, and that is in parentheses, rights, not understanding what they were. If there was, in fact, this misunderstanding of the law and if, in fact, that was a material part of the proceeding -- caused a material effect in the proceeding, then we can fix it. We can fix it now. We do not have to wait -- in the case of my client this means fifteen years -- to fix it. We can fix it right now. Thank you, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Actually when we concluded in the Mucic case and subsequently applications came tumbling in, actually I thought it was understood that what was being discussed in each case was whether a statement made by a suspect under certain conditions of coercion, fraud or force could be rejected on those grounds. This was, I thought, the common law Rule. If that was the case, these factors have to be tried, and the prosecution which took the statements has to justify that there was no such coercion or fraud. This is the understanding in the common law world about trying a statement which has been tainted with these vices. What I now hear, what is being submitted to the Trial Chamber, are matters going beyond a question of the validity of the statements themselves which were voluntarily made. What is being argued is the motive for the voluntariness, why it was voluntary. That is quite a different matter from whether, in fact, anybody induced the accused or suspect to do certain things. I do not know. This might be a new aspect of it all, but I think it is fairly different from the general rule. I admit the contention and especially when you talk about the position of the prosecution. At least those who come from the common law experience, and I hear Mr. Christmas Humphries, as he put it, wanting justice first, justice second, conviction a very bad third, I think this is what everybody wants. Nobody goes at conviction as a major factor. It should be what the facts themselves disclose. From the arguments which we have heard you are going beyond the question of whether these witnesses were induced to give this evidence or were coerced to give these statements. They are quite different things. I do not know. We still have to rule on the matter despite what it is. It might be fairly difficult to talk about the question of voluntariness outside the grounds on which it has now been raised, because what Judge Ackerman has been stressing is perhaps the suspect did not have the best advice, so he was unable to give the best opinion which enabled him to exercise his choices. This is what I understand it to mean. If he had got the best advice or the appropriate advice, he would have exercised his options properly. He would not have made the statements as he has done. It appears that Mr. Moran is not too far away from that same approach. That is what their clients understood from their background, and what they were familiar with was quite different from what we call it, and the result is they were making decisions unfamiliar with what they were required to do. Now I do not know how the Rules could have known and then particularly allowed every accused person to carry his own law around him. It was not so done. What the Rules state was to formulate a general rule which could be applicable to everybody who came before the Tribunal, or who is affected by the exercise of jurisdiction by the Tribunal. This is what they convey and this is why we have our provisions even up to Rule 95, allowing evidence which was obtained improperly under current international law to be retracted, if it became necessary. That is quite different from whether the evidence itself was voluntarily made. It could be voluntarily made but it could be excluded if it contravened all the internationally made human right provisions. That is a different thing. (Pause). Gentlemen, I think we will give a Ruling when we come back after the break. So we will now hear counsel for Mucic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Your Honours, what I have got to say is -- I am sorry. My learned friend has popped up. She plainly has something urgent to tell us.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, if it is the case that Mr. Greaves is going to speak to the actual motion about these statements, I would just state that the prosecution has not responded in part because it goes into details about what happened in Austria and Austrian law, and we anticipate that we will be able to have a full and complete response by the end of this week, and we do not believe that it is necessary for this Chamber to decide Mr. Mucic's motion at this moment. We are -- after witness O we are going to have a witness who, because of the -- one, because of the severe allegation made, we want to clarify at least one part of what happened, which is what happened -- what the Office of the Prosecutor did, but with respect to the full evidence about this, including subsequent events and even potentially what happened with respect to the Viennese authorities, that may require a little time. So obviously we will respond as much as we are able to whatever Mr. Greaves says about that issue, but with respect to our full response, we would be requesting at the minimum to supplement our response later on. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Actually, my understanding, and I think it is the correct law, is when such an allegation has been made about certain things done to his client, it is for you to justify that those things have not been done. All the evidence necessary to show us that the witness made his statement voluntarily, he was not induced to do it, will be produced by you, and all counsel needs to do is to cross-examine you to show that it was not voluntary.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. I was not disagreeing with that or that procedure. I was just saying with respect to certain -- and I was not suggesting that he was obligated to put on evidence about this matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Thank you. The matters raised by my learned friend bring me to the end of what I was going to say first rather than later. If I can explain this: the contention that we have is that the process by which certain oral statements were procured from the defendant Mucic by the Office of the Prosecution are affected not just by allegations that I have to make to OTP investigators but by the whole of what had happened from the moment of his arrest on 18th March, and that involves the procedures of the Austrian Police and the Austrian courts, and then the sudden switch from the procedures and rights advised to him by the courts there -- the sudden switch to the procedures of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence that are applicable to interviews by the officer of the prosecution under rules 42 and 43. So the position is this, and I have tried to explain this to the prosecution, and I fear that they have not understood it. As your Lordship will recall, I addressed you last week on what I considered, and I hoped was going to be taken on board, the appropriate way in which to adduce evidence and for the issue of the admissibility of these statements to be tried by your Honours. The only way in which your Honours are going logically to be able to understand the points that are raised by the defendant Mr. Mucic, and I on his behalf, are by hearing the case, the evidence, in proper chronological order. If the prosecution call Mr. Abribat and Mr. d'Hooge out of order before the Austrian police officer, your Honours are not going to understand this motion for a moment. It is simply going to be completely incomprehensible. I say that because I spent yesterday in the City of Vienna in the company of distinguished lawyers of the Austrian Bar. Firstly, there are matters of law that are going to have to be placed before your Honours, and I say to the prosecution now I anticipate, I hope, being able to designate an Austrian lawyer as an expert witness, who can assist your Honours, because you are going to need assistance as to what Austrian law is and what rights are accorded to persons who are arrested and accused, so that your Honours may better understand the state of mind of the defendant and also apply Rules 89D and Rule 95. Without hearing such evidence, your Honours are not going to be able to rule properly on this motion, a motion which is based both in law and in fact. Secondly, there are two witnesses as to fact whom I have discovered. I have not yet had an opportunity to take from either of those witnesses a witness statement in connection with matters which took place in Vienna. Until I am in possession of such a statement, I am not in a position to cross-examine properly either Mr. Abribat or Mr. d'Hooge. There will be matters -- it may be neither of those witnesses helps me, but until I know what the position is, I simply cannot properly advance the case for the defendant. Thirdly, this morning I know -- and I am not criticising the prosecution in any way -- it was by mischance that material was placed in the wrong locker for the court for me. I can hold it up for your Honours to see. (Indicating). It is that thick. It concerns events that took place at Vienna. Although much of it was translated, it was given to me shortly before your Honours came into court this morning. I simply have not had time to digest or understand what is contained in here or consider the implications of these documents and what implications they may have for my motion that I have placed before the court. It may be that I would have to either amend or add to the motion to make it more comprehensible for your Honours. The next matter is this, and I now return to where I started, it is the proper procedure for determining the admissibility of Mr. Mucic's statement to the Austrian Police and the statements which he made to the Office of the Prosecution. There has been some discussion in previous motions as to the way in which one holds a voir dire. I am sure that both your Honours, who come from common law jurisdictions, will recall the procedure in trials for those before your Honour's courts in practice and as members of the judiciary. When an issue of admissibility is raised, the usual procedure in the common law jurisdictions, and I am sorry to harp on about common law jurisdictions to the disadvantage of my civil law colleagues across the way, but I hope you will bear with me for a moment, the procedure is this: when the prosecution seeks to adduced contested evidence, evidence that is contested as to its admissibility, it should call that evidence and hear cross-examination of its own witness. There is then an opportunity, if so advised, for the defence to call evidence, and it is called a trial within a trial. So it is a trial of an issue , to call evidence on his own behalf as to what took place. That is the procedure that I urge on the court as being the most expeditious and fair way to dispose of this matter. I say that because my submission to the court is this: the only way in which this court can properly and justly determine the issue of admissibility is to hear the prosecution's witnesses on this issue in a proper and logical order; otherwise your Honours are simply going to be left in the dark. If your Honours are left in the dark, my client is not going to get justice. My submission to your Honours is that I know the prosecution are anxious to get on with their evidence, but I have noted in one of the motions or documents that has been served through the court this morning that they are keen for this evidence to be heard as soon as possible. I ask this question: what is the hurry? Why do we need to hurry this procedure? I have raised what is a prima facie and serious matter. The prosecution seem determined that it should be heard with unseemly haste. I would respectfully suggest to your Honours that you must now control the adducing of this evidence in a way that is just and proper and is best designed to assist your Honours to determine the issue fairly and properly, both in the interests of the defendant and, let me say it, in the interests of the prosecution. I am not sure that they have understood the help that I have tried to give them, and help I have tried to do. It is not in my interest to try to pull a trick on them or a fast one in any way. I have tried to help them to understand how to do it in order for you to determine it, and it may be you determine in the prosecution's favour. I know not. Unless it is done properly, a serious triable issue is going to be tried badly and unjustly. My submission is quite clear: this matter should not be heard now. It should be heard in its proper way by the court. I support what is said about the question of Austrian law and it is plain that this matter in its totality has not been prepared either by the prosecution or by myself. I make that quite plain. Some of the advice I was given yesterday by an Austrian lawyer is in German. Amongst my many accomplishments is not a full knowledge of the German language I have to tell you. So there are documents in German I have to have translated and upon which I have to get advice from someone who is qualified to give it, namely an Austrian lawyer. I am simply not in a position to advance this motion on the defendant's behalf properly, and I would ask your Honours to say that this matter should be put back so that a proper timescale can be achieved for it, so that it can be tried properly and justly in the interests of both this court and the interests of the defendant and in the interests of the prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I respond to that? The prosecution is not proceeding with unseemly haste. To the contrary, we have a situation where the accused's defence has made a very serious allegation about the voluntary nature of his client's waiver, some of which may have to do with exactly what happened in Austrian proceedings and it may, although we will not concede this point, it may -- at least the defence may want to bring some specifics of Austrian law which we are not familiar with, and I, in fact, believe will argue are not controlling, but he has not argued them. He has also made an allegation about the conduct of the Office of the Prosecutor. It is the case that the Office of the Prosecutor does want to act with haste to get that issue clarified, so that there is no allegation -- so that the evidence supports that the Office of the Prosecutor has not acted improperly or unfairly. I understand that this issue -- that all of this issue may not be resolved immediately, but the prosecution has at great trouble, given this allegation, brought in the Chief Investigator who was in Vienna, who will not be able -- he is not an expert on Austrian procedure and Austrian law and he may not know all that. Certainly he will be able to testify about what the Office of the Prosecutor did and how they handled themselves and show that the Office of the Prosecutor acted properly and fairly in all respects. He is no longer with the Tribunal. He flew in this morning. He has to fly out again tomorrow. We wish to call him today after witness O, who also has his own scheduling problems, and if it is then necessary for the Chamber -- for the defence to recall him at some later time, of course that can be done, but what he has information about is what happened with respect to the Office of the Prosecutor. We wish to present that evidence. We believe it is the right of the prosecution to determine the manner in which it calls its witnesses, subject to supervision by your Honours, and we very much appreciate the advice given by Mr. Greaves concerning how we should conduct our case, and, like certain decisions, it may turn out not to be correct, but it is our considered opinion that we wish to dispel any notion immediately that the Office of the Prosecutor has acted improperly, and we wish to immediately call after witness O Mr. Abribat. If your Honours later decide that it is necessary for your understanding to call him back again, or the defence decides to do that, of course that is possible. We do not anticipate that it will be necessary, but if it turns out that we were wrong, there is, in effect, no harm done, and we believe it is our right, even our duty, to clarify the matter as soon as possible, given the allegations made by defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: This is a matter between the two of you, the prosecution and the defence, and I think the burden is greater on the part of the prosecution, whose duty it is to prove that the statement they took was voluntary. So in every case you have to liaise with the defence to know how you organise the arguments.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Can I say this, your Honour: if my learned friend calls Mr. Abribat shortly, I shall apply for an adjournment. I am not fully in possession of the information I need to cross-examine him, and it is going to waste your Honours' time, in my submission. I can well understand the prosecution do not like allegations being made about the conduct of their investigators, but in the real and robust world such allegations are frequently made in courts all over this continent and on other continents, and they are allegations which do not get tried for quite some time. It does not affect the integrity of the prosecution in any way, that one small part of their operation is called into question, and I do not suggest in any way that the allegations I have to make impugns other investigators who are not concerned with my client or any members of the prosecution team. So the desire to remove this alleged stain with the haste that is being proposed is one which is not necessary to do. This issue must be tried properly and must be tried by the case being placed before you in proper order, so that you can understand it. You will have to trust me. Hearing this evidence out of order and in the way that you are being invited is going to make it impossible for you to understand what is going on. I cannot, with the greatest of respect to my learned friend, see what the urgency is. There is no proper justification, in my submission, for hurrying this important issue. I was only aware, although it was at my invitation, when I arrived at court that Mr. Abribat had been placed on the prosecution's witness list. I do not object to him being on the list, but it was perhaps unfortunate that the prosecution have chosen to fly him in specially in the knowledge of what I had suggested to them and what my likely response was to be, as it has been this morning, to the proposition that he should give evidence straightaway. In my submission it was premature of them to fly him in and unwise, but they may need to reflect on that. I revert to my principal submission, which I invite your Honours to consider, and I would respectfully say that in the interests of justice, and that is, after all, why we are all here, your Honour should adopt the propositions that I have placed before you as to the proper conduct of this case. Of course my learned friend says it is up to the prosecution in very large part to determine how and what evidence they call, but at the end of the day the residual discretion lies in this Honourable Tribunal to control its own proceedings, control its own proceedings so that the persons sitting on that Tribunal, your Honours, can properly try the issues laid before it. That may require the giving of directions by this court as to how and when a particular issue will be tried. That is a process that I am sure all of your Honours are familiar with, and it is a process which I respectfully invite your Honours to say is appropriate for the proper determination of the serious issue that I have raised, and I invite your Honours to accept the propositions that I have placed before you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Mr. Greaves, do you not think that at the time you were making the allegations you were cognisant with the facts to support such allegation, so that if anyone was brought before you for trying those statements, then you would be able to justify them?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I thought I had in my possession 100 per cent of the facts. It was only as a result of going to Vienna yesterday that I became aware of some completely new matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Although I have spoken to the partner of a lawyer who may or may not be able to be a witness as to facts, I have not actually spoken to that actual person, because he was in Salzburg dealing with a matter of considerable importance of his own in his own professional conduct. The simple answer is, since last speaking to your Honours, I have become aware of other things, and it is for that reason that I have made this application today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: We will consider how best to deal with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: I think the Trial Chamber will rise now and reassemble at 12 o'clock.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: We will start with our Ruling on the two motions. I think we will take them together, since ideally the same conditions are applicable to them. We have reviewed the motions themselves and discussed amongst ourselves. The Trial Chamber will give a more reasoned Ruling later, but for now we are satisfied that the procedural requirements for admitting these statements were not violated and therefore they could be admissible at this stage. Now whether the parties actually tendering the statements met the substantial requirements about the validity themselves can be raised and challenged, but as statements for what happened at that time they are clearly admissible. As I said earlier, the basis for going to -- trying a statement has not been established. None of the grounds which have been put forward before us suggested any fraud or coercion or force in the obtaining of the statements, but whether those statements meet the standards required is a different matter. I think that is all for now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: At the end of the trial, when the entire evidence is before the Tribunal, it will be open to the defence to argue that these statements should be excluded from consideration as the safeguards provided in the Rules have not in substance been complied with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes. Can we hear you, Mr. Ostberg?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Thank you. Yesterday, your Honour, we filed a motion on protection for a person formerly named. I asked for him to be given the pseudonym of Mr. O. I would now like to call this witness and ask for your Honours to rule on our request for protection before I do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, we were served with this some time after -- I received it some time after 9 o'clock this morning in a stack of documents. I have seen the name witness O about three or four times spread through these documents and nobody has bothered to tell me who the heck witness O is. I would really like to know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: That, of course, I cannot do in open court. If we enter private session, I will immediately tell everybody who it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: But have you not given the defence earlier the material, the particulars identifying the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: I have indeed, your Honour. The question is that when this witness appears in The Hague and I meet him, he asks and gives reasons for asking for protection, and I could not say no to such a proposition, and that is why I filed this motion. I could not have done it earlier, because I was not informed of his concerns about his security until he arrived in The Hague. So there has been no other way for me to do it, and I cannot even apologise to the defence for the late disclosure of this thing, because I had no idea myself before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: In all seriousness did you ever try to speak to the defence about it, knowing the sudden way in which you are springing him?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Just a moment. (Pause). I am informed from my case manager that yesterday every defence lawyer, lead defence lawyer, was informed over the phone of this, but we were not able to reach Mr. Karabdic. That is why I have the objection of Mr. Moran, I suppose, but we tried twice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: But you know the identity of the witness and you know the substance of the evidence which the witness is going to give?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, before the break Ms. McHenry mentioned a title that attached to witness O, and that gives me a hint, and if it is who I think it is, there is two problems. One was at 9.45 -- we had had five pages of statement from this witness. At 9.45 this morning I was handed a total of fifteen pages, which included five pages with some big black X marks on it. Secondly, if it is the witness that I think it is, I have filed a motion which may need to be marked confidential, because his name is in it, an objection to appearance of undesignated expert witnesses. If it is the person I think it is, in the material I was handed this morning there is a lot of things in Latin, having to do with medical diagnoses, and frankly, judge, high school was a long time ago. My Latin is not nearly as good as it was then and it was not very good back then. I have got ten pages' worth of things I have never seen before in my life. It is possible that these things were served in Bosnian on the Bosnian lawyers, but I do not speak Bosnian at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: What you are really asking is not that the identity should not be disclosed or the evidence should not be taken in public, but that his evidence should not be recorded at all today, because you are not prepared?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Well, your Honour, there are two things: one, the Trial Chamber on January 25th of this year entered an Order on expert witnesses, which I am prepared to argue. Basically what it said is you have to get a CV, you have to tell us what it is about, that kind of thing. We have complied with it. There is a provision for good cause which we have actually filed a motion on. The Trial Chamber has not ruled on it yet but something came up during the trial. We need an expert. We gave as much notice as we could. I think that you have to draw a distinction between a fact witness and an expert witness; an expert witness is giving opinions, testifying because of special expertise, and a fact witness, who says: "I saw this". These people -- as I recall, there were only two people that were designated as expert witness. The one was Dr Calic and the other one is a Dutch general, whose name escapes me at the moment. Just because someone is a professional person does not necessarily mean he is going to be giving opinion testimony or he is going to be testifying from special expertise. If this person -- and it appears from the documents that I was handed this morning that he is going to be testifying concerning special expertise based on his training and experience -- we would like to know who the heck this man is. I would like to run him through some computers to see if he has ever published anything, that kind of thing, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: He is an expert witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: I have the answer to all of this, your Honours. We do not consider him an expert witness. He appears on our witness list, where we do include his name, as number 12. Under number 12 he is named for the defence and also the court is put on notice as to what he is going to testify to. As to the knowledge of the defence lawyers, I am utterly surprised, because defence was given a full set of what he is going to talk about in the court on dates which I can specify, and everyone got notice of it in due time during 1996, and everyone received a full set of what it is all about, everyone but Mr. Karabdic, who instead inspected them on 25th July 1996. English translations, they were given in original -- copies of the original, and English translation was received in full sets on 4th March 1997 to Mr. Karabdic,. Mr. Brackovic received a full set on 19th February 1997. Mr. Tapuskovic never asked for a translation but was put on notice what it was and knew what it was. Mme Residovic received nine reports which were then being translated but had before been given a full set of it in Serbo-Croatian, which is the language of her own and her client. So the prosecution has done everything that it could possibly do to give the defence notice of what we are going to do here. As a service to the defence lawyers, we have now provided them with a list in English of all the things I am going to ask the witness about, to be provided to them maybe today. This is to be looked on as a clear service. All disclosure asked for in the Rules has been provided in due time. So I am stunned about this objection. I cannot understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would be happy to show the Trial Chamber, one, what I had in my file relating to this person I think is witness O as of 9 o'clock this morning, and then what I was handed at 9.45. I have got them both in my hand. One is a five-page document. One is a fifteen-page document. If I was given just a partial one, then I do not know quite what to say. The fact is that looking at page 5 of the two sets of documents, they are not identical in that page 5 that I have, the older one, as the Trial Chamber can see, has just one notation on it, and the one that I was handed this morning, as the Trial Chamber can see, has two. Even if there is some kind of mistake in copying, there is something wrong with this picture.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: There is nothing wrong with them. They are just put together in another order. The translations, some of them has been improved, I suppose, but the originals are in Serbo-Croat. The person to be examined in this court is to be examined in that language. He has written in his own language. We have speakers of this language sitting on the defence bench. There can be no misunderstanding whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, the last time I looked at the Statute, the two official languages of this Tribunal are English and French. Serbo-Croatian is not one of them. As I pointed out, I speak absolutely no Serbo-Croatian, read less, and the fact that something was served in Serbo-Croatian I do not know complies with the Statute and the Rules.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: But you are a member of a team.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: That is true, your Honour, and I will happily stipulate that my lead counsel is quite fluent in Serbo-Croatian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: One other thing is this morning at about 9 o'clock I received a change in order of witness list, which apparently changes the order in which this particular witness was going to appear. We were expecting, when we left here on Thursday, the next witness to be Bart d'Hooge, and I walk in this morning and find, on somebody else's desk, I might add -- it was put in somebody else's box by accident and handed to me after 9 o'clock this morning -- a motion to change the witness list. At some point if we are going to require witness lists and we are going to require that people have notice of when witnesses are going to appear so you can prepare for cross, you have got to have some time to do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: I have an observation to that too, your Honour, if I may. I am certain that the prosecution -- the defence will experience when it comes to the defence case the same logistic and other problems we cope with every day. This makes it necessary when bringing in witnesses from other parts of the world to try to put this together in a feasible way not to interfere all too much in their professional or private life. So we have to, and you will do that in the same order when time comes -- we have to do changes in our witnesses. I cannot help it, your Honour, even if we try hard to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: There is no right for the defence to follow a witness list as I understand it under the Procedures adopted by this Trial Chamber. We can call witnesses in any order we want. There was, however, an order entered, I believe on 25th January, and do not hold me to that, about witness lists and the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I might add for Esad Landzo at this point that we did only actively and constructively receive notice of the change of the witness schedule this morning at 9.45 before court resumed. We attended this proceeding today thinking that the next witness was going to be Bart d'Hooge instead of witness number O, and it will highly prejudice this case if we are expected to perform and be prepared to cross-examine a witness that we were not expecting for several days from now at this point. Also, the changing of the witness list is one thing, but the protection of this witness that they are seeking I believe requires a hearing on this. At this point if the prosecution insist behind closed doors, because we have no reason to suspect why this person, who we are still not sure who it is -- we have never been notified exactly who Witness O is at this point -- we have never received notice of who Witness O is according to this document that we received. It just says "Witness O". Other than what Ms. McHenry -- the clue she gave us this morning -- we do not know who that person is. So according to the schedule that we appeared on today, we were expecting Bart d'Hooge to be the next witness. All of a sudden Witness O is brought in to testify today. We are caught by surprise and will not be prepared to cross-examine that witness if he is allowed to go out of order today. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: But are you not aware of the identity of Witness O?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: No, your Honour. We have never been provided with the knowledge of who Witness O is.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Lead counsel for Mr. Esad Landzo was informed yesterday at 2 o'clock.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
